title: The broken tusk
hookLine: Ganesha snaps his tusk to keep writing the Mahabharata; why learning is sacred and writers begin with him
carry: learning is sacred; ganesha gave a tusk
tomorrow: a god this big gets around on what, exactly?
last: CIRCLE YOUR PARENTS LIKE A TEMPLE.

lines: A POEM TOO BIG TO HOLD.
cards: Look at a Ganesha statue and count the tusks. One is whole. The other is snapped short, and often he's holding the broken piece in his hand.

Behind that tusk is a writer's story. The sage Vyasa has a vast poem in his head, the Mahabharata, the epic that holds Krishna's battlefield line from day twenty-one, and he needs someone to write it down as he speaks.
Ganesha says yes, on one condition: once I start, you can't stop. Vyasa adds his own: you can't write a line until you understand it. They begin.
Somewhere in the middle, with the poem nowhere near done, the pen breaks.

teach.b: He can't stop; that was his own rule. So, the story goes, he snaps off his own tusk, dips it in the ink and keeps writing. That's one reason he's called Ekadanta, the one with one tusk.

A fact worth knowing: this scribe scene appears in some versions of the Mahabharata, but the modern critical edition, built by comparing manuscripts, leaves it out, and some Puranas explain the tusk with a fight against the warrior-sage Parashurama.
So hold it as a story, not a record. But look at what Hindus took from it. Ganesha isn't only the remover of obstacles.

teach.h: LORD OF LEARNING AND THE WRITTEN WORD.
teach.b: He's the lord of wisdom and learning, the god of the written word. In Hinduism, knowledge is holy: words that teach you how to live are worth a piece of a god. And Vyasa's rule matters too.
Ganesha may not write a line he doesn't understand.

teach.h: LEARNING IS SACRED; GANESHA GAVE A TUSK.
teach.b: Sacred learning isn't speed; it's understanding. That's why many Hindu students, writers and shopkeepers open a new notebook or account book by writing Shri Ganesh at the top.
In Kerala, at a ceremony called Vidyarambham, a small child's very first written words often begin with a prayer to Ganapati. Learning starts with him.

how: Ganesha is honored as the lord of wisdom and learning. Many Hindus write Shri Ganesh or a line honoring him at the top of a new notebook or account book, and at Vidyarambham in Kerala a child's first written letters often begin with a prayer to Ganapati.

games.why: Ekadanta gave part of himself so sacred words got written down. other tellings have a fight with Parashurama, and Hindus honor him as lord of learning either way.

practice: Find a pen and a page. If you pray, write Shri Ganesh at the top, the way many Hindus open a new notebook; if you don't, write one word for what you're grateful to have learned.
Under it, write one thing you've learned this month, from this app, a book or a person, in your own words. Write it only once you're sure you understand it: that was Vyasa's rule.
Then read it back slowly, like something worth keeping.

wordCard.voice: Ekadanta, from eka, one, and danta, tooth or tusk: the name Ganesha earned by giving his own tusk to the written word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one (eka) tooth or tusk (danta), one of Ganesha's names.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: learning is sacred; Ganesha gave a tusk for it. Twenty-six days in.
